news.title: Trump says he is talking to Russia and China about denuclearization
news.text:
WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump said on Thursday Washington is holding talks with ​Moscow and Beijing aimed at denuclearizing ‌the countries with the biggest stockpiles of nuclear weapons.

Russia has the most stored nuclear warheads followed by ​the United States and China, according to ​the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. The ⁠US outpaces Russia on its number of ​deployed warheads.

During an interview with Newsmax, Trump said ​he expects China to “catch up” with the US within the next five years.

“The whole thing is a shame, ​because I’d love to denuclearize if possible, ​but we’re actually talking to Russia about that, and ‌we’re ⁠talking to China about that denuclearization,” Trump told the outlet.

Newsmax reported that Trump had spoken with Chinese President Xi Jinping about denuclearization.

Trump’s comments ​come months ​after the ⁠Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty expired earlier this year.

The New START treaty signed ​in 2010 allowed one single extension, which ​was ⁠agreed by former President Joe Biden and Russian President Vladimir Putin for five years. Any ⁠new ​extension would require an executive ​decision to voluntarily extend the limits of the treaty.

news.text:
WASHINGTON: New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said on Thursday she did ​not pass the bar exam after facing scrutiny ‌about her legal career before becoming the top spokeswoman for US President Donald Trump.

Zacharia, who joined the White House on Monday, has previously ​said she practiced law before entering politics and ​Trump had described her as an attorney.

“You did ⁠not pass the bar exam, correct?” she was asked ​in an interview on Fox News’ “Hannity” show late on Thursday.

“Correct,” ​she said in response to the host, Sean Hannity.

“I did not,” she said when Hannity asked if she ever took the bar ​exam a second time.

Zacharia earned her law degree from ​Pepperdine University in 2011, according to the university. Nearly all licensed US ‌lawyers ⁠first obtain a law degree, but law school graduates cannot legally practice law in the US without first being admitted to a state bar.

When asked about her performance by Hannity, she said: “What I feel is I ⁠really ​stepped up to the plate to ​do the press conference, Sean, with very little prep time.”

news.title: Jesse Watters Skewers ‘Off-Putting’ Must-Win Trump Candidate
news.text:
Jesse Watters has a problem with the President Donald Trump’s Senate pick in Texas, and it’s not just his politics.

The Fox News host, 48, took aim at Ken Paxton on Thursday’s The Five. 

The panel was discussing the race between the 69-year-old and his Democrat opponent, James Talarico, when Watters chimed in. 

Talarico, 37, is a progressive populist and is joining the party’s rising progressive wing. Billionaires are a primary target. He even bought a Super Bowl ad declaring that “billionaires don’t just influence politicians, they own them,” Bloomberg Law reported.

Watters went after Paxton while his co-hosts tore into Talarico.

Co-host Emily Compagno, 47, accused Talarico of softening his left-wing views on abortion and trans issues to win over Texans.

“Like any way you slice it, he appears either weak or horrifying, right?” she asked. Talarico spent years championing trans rights in the Texas legislature. But since winning the nomination, he has backed away from some of his positions, The Washington Post reported.

Watters responded, saying there’s “something off-putting” about the Texas attorney general just days before Texans start voting, in a race where a Fox News poll shows Talarico narrowly ahead.

“But he’s running against Paxton, and Paxton has a lazy eye,” he said, looking dubious. 

“And this whiff of corruption around [him], even though he was like the best attorney general in the country for the last eight years, there’s just something off-putting about him.”

Paxton has suffered a string of leaks before in the must-win race. A leaked campaign memo warned donors that Talarico holds the advantage on the airwaves, with $65 million in ads spent or reserved at cheaper rates than Paxton’s team can get. In September, audio was leaked from a private Washington fundraiser catching Paxton blaming Trump’s Dallas convention for sinking his numbers.

Last week, The New York Times published a leaked 2014 deposition from a federal fraud probe. In it, Paxton told SEC lawyers he couldn’t recall details more than 200 times and blamed his tax returns on his now-estranged wife. Days later, The Wall Street Journal reported claims that Paxton spent New Year’s Eve 2024 partying in Dubai with his girlfriend and two men charged with healthcare fraud in the U.S.

On The Five, Watters said the unease about Paxton was coming up in his own conversations. He recounted speaking with a man in neighboring Oklahoma who told him Texans were souring on both men.

“I’m hearing from a lot of people in Texas that they’re definitely not voting for Talarico, but they’re still having trouble bringing themselves to vote for Paxton,” Watters said, relaying the man’s words.

Watters said he then checked in with “my guy,” a Paxton mega donor, who pointed to private polling.

“They still think Paxton wins by about two or three,” Watters said.

Then he turned his fire back on Talarico.

“So you know, between the veganism, the gay rumors, being against capitalism and global warming and fantasizing about trans kids, this guy just can’t cut it in Texas,” Watters said, mixing digs at Talarico’s politics with baseless rumors about his personal life that MAGA figures have pushed for months.

In the same breath, however, he conceded that only one thing was keeping Republicans afloat: cash.

“Thank God we have more money than they do or else this could be curtains for Republicans,” he said.

Paxton’s campaign and Talarico’s campaign did not immediately respond to the Daily Beast’s requests for comment.

Texans head to the polls on Election Day, Nov. 3, with early voting kicking off Monday.

news.title: Israel raises alert amid Iran war fears as Trump weighs strikes, Netanyahu wary before election
news.text: Israel has raised its military alert level and is preparing for the possibility of renewed fighting with Iran at short notice, but Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and senior defense officials remain reluctant to initiate another military campaign ahead of the October 27 election. The heightened readiness comes as U.S. President Donald Trump leaves open the possibility of additional strikes against Iran, raising concerns that a miscalculation could trigger a war neither Israel nor Tehran necessarily intended to start. The IDF is closely monitoring developments in Iran and preparing for a rapid return to combat if necessary. Tehran, meanwhile, is working to rebuild its military capabilities, strengthen its defenses and prepare for another possible confrontation with Israel and the United States. However, Iranian military preparations do not necessarily indicate that an attack is imminent, nor do they automatically justify an Israeli preemptive strike. Conversations with Israeli defense officials suggest that Netanyahu, who has publicly said Israel does not intend to initiate another war, is also unenthusiastic about launching a new offensive against Iran in internal discussions. With less than two weeks remaining before the election, officials are struggling to identify a clear strategic objective that could justify the costs of another war and produce a meaningful result within such a short period. The killing of Iran's former supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, has already taken place. A decisive blow to Iran's nuclear program could constitute another major strategic achievement, but beyond that, there is currently no obvious objective of comparable importance that could be achieved quickly enough to fundamentally change the situation. More importantly, Israeli officials do not appear to see an immediate threat so urgent that military action cannot wait another two weeks. Even the assumption that Israel could launch a limited operation, achieve its objectives and quickly return to normal life is being treated with caution. Israel can decide how to begin a military campaign, but it cannot determine on its own how Iran will respond or when the fighting will end. Tehran could choose a much broader response in an effort to restore deterrence against Israel and the United States, turning a limited strike into a prolonged confrontation. The consequences could be severe, including missile attacks on Israel's home front, disruptions to economic activity, substantial military costs and fighting on additional fronts. Another escalation could also significantly affect civilian life and the country's ability to conduct its upcoming election under normal conditions. That raises a difficult question for Israel's political and military leadership: If there is no immediate threat requiring action, is it worth risking another major war just days before Israelis head to the polls? Trump's latest remarks add to the uncertainty Much of the calculation, however, may ultimately depend on decisions made in Washington rather than Jerusalem. Trump's latest comments have reinforced the possibility that the United States could resume military operations against Iran even as Israel remains cautious about initiating another confrontation. In an interview with Newsmax on Thursday, Trump discussed the possibility of additional strikes against Iranian nuclear facilities, including a heavily fortified site known as Pickaxe Mountain. "Now, we're looking at Pickaxe Mountain. We may have to go there," Trump said. "We'll take a shot at that one. We'll knock it out fast." His remarks came against the backdrop of a CNN report that the U.S. military has developed new strike plans that include the possible use of the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, commonly known as the "mother of all bombs," against Iranian nuclear sites and energy infrastructure. The massive conventional weapon is designed primarily to produce a devastating surface blast rather than penetrate facilities buried deep underground, raising questions about its effectiveness against heavily fortified nuclear installations. Trump did not rule out using the weapon, but emphasized that it is not nuclear. "Well, the mother of all bombs is not nuclear," he said. "No, it's not nuclear at all. This is just an extremely large bomb," he added. The president also dismissed the prospect of deploying American ground troops inside Iran. "No, I don't see that. I don't see that," he said when asked about the possibility. At the same time, Trump suggested that negotiations with Tehran were continuing and that Iranian officials had requested a halt to American and Israeli attacks. "They've asked us to please stop. And we do, because we're negotiating with them," he said. Trump also addressed his relationship with Netanyahu during the interview. Asked whether he trusted the Israeli prime minister, he replied, "I don't trust anybody, honestly," clarifying that he meant politics generally rather than singling out Netanyahu. He went on to praise their cooperation, saying, "Look, I've had a very good relationship with him. We've had good success together." The president also claimed that Israelis would like him involved in the October 27 election, although he stopped short of committing to participate in Netanyahu's campaign. For Israeli defense planners, the more pressing question is what Trump might decide regarding Iran. If the American president concludes that U.S. interests require renewed military action, particularly amid Saudi Arabia's security concerns and fears of Iranian aggression, Israel's strategic calculations could change substantially. The prevailing assessment is that another large-scale confrontation would likely involve close operational coordination between Israel and the United States, rather than separate military campaigns. Whether Trump will ultimately authorize another offensive, however, remains uncertain. Hezbollah could also join a renewed confrontation, as it did during the previous round of fighting known as Operation Roaring Lion. Israeli planners must account for that possibility, although Hezbollah's participation would not necessarily determine the outcome of the conflict. Above all, the danger of miscalculation remains. Israel is increasing its military readiness because of concerns about Iran, but Tehran could interpret those measures as preparations for an imminent Israeli attack. Both sides are taking precautions to avoid being caught off guard, yet those preparations could themselves create the conditions for escalation. A localized incident, a faulty intelligence assessment or a military response perceived as disproportionate could ignite a wider confrontation without either side having made a deliberate decision to go to war. That is the central dilemma facing Israel's leadership. Military readiness is essential in the face of the Iranian threat, but preparing for war does not necessarily mean that launching one is justified. Any decision to initiate another offensive would require a clear objective, an assessment of its likely costs and a realistic understanding of how the fighting might end. The question is not simply whether Israel is capable of fighting another war, but what it could achieve through military action that cannot be achieved by other means. As long as no clear strategic objective justifies the potential costs, choosing not to strike should not be mistaken for weakness. For now, the combination of Israeli military preparations, Iranian efforts to rebuild its defenses and Trump's willingness to consider additional strikes has created a particularly sensitive situation. Whether the current tensions remain a contest of deterrence or develop into another regional war may ultimately depend on decisions made in Washington, Jerusalem and Tehran, or on a single miscalculation that none of them anticipated.
news.summary: With the IDF preparing for renewed fighting, Netanyahu sees no clear strategic objective for another offensive before October 27; Trump's latest threats against Iran add uncertainty, while Israeli officials fear a miscalculation could trigger a wider war

news.title: Trump Goes to Desperate Efforts for His Must-Win MAGA Candidate
news.text:
President Donald Trump has pointed his finger at two of his Republican foes in a desperate attempt to steer voting back to his must-win candidate. 

Texas Attorney General Paxton, 63, is in a tight Senate race with Democrat James Talarico, 37. The last Democrat elected to the Senate from Texas was Lloyd Bentsen in 1988.

Three polls released this week have Talarico in the lead, as much as by four points, according to ReconMR/Siena calculations. Election site Decision Desk gives Talarico a 56 percent chance to flip the Texas Senate seat.

Trump endorsed scandal-ridden Paxton over incumbent Senator John Cornyn in May, and strategically held the Republican National Midterm Convention in Dallas last month, where he continued to throw his support behind Paxton.

However, as Paxton struggles in the polls, Trump has already flagged he will blame Cornyn and former White House adviser Karl Rove if his pick loses, while pleading with voters to switch to Paxton.

“Sadly, and very stupidly, John Cornyn, and his Liddle’ Buddy, Super RINO, Karl Rove, are doing everything possible to make it hard for Ken Paxton, the Greatest Attorney General in the History of Texas, and one of the Best in the United States, to win the upcoming Midterm Election against a Radical Left Lunatic, James TalaFREAKO, who is the ANTITHESIS of Texas Values,” Trump vented on Truth Social on Thursday.

The president claimed Cornyn “lost the Primary to Ken by a very wide margin” after he endorsed Paxton, and insisted Rove “shouldn’t be allowed to spew his jealously on FoxNews,” then added they “should be ashamed of themselves.”

Paxton won the Republican primary in May, ending three decades of Cornyn’s electoral dominance. Paxton took home 63.8 percent of the votes compared to Cornyn’s 36.2, according to the Texas Tribune.

Strategist Rove declared in a Wall Street Journal opinion piece last month that he would vote for Democrat Jon Rosenthal over Republican Bo French in the race for a seat on the Texas Railroad Commission. “The GOP’s stables need a cleaning,” he wrote, adding it was only the second time he has ever voted for a Democrat. “This is a good place to start.”

Rove has been a political contributor to the president’s favorite network, Fox News, since 2008.

Stating the pair are hurting both Texas and the U.S., Trump said in his Truth Social post Thursday, “If Ken Paxton loses, it will be because of WEAK and INEFFECTIVE Political Hacks like John Cornyn and Karl Rove, who have ineffectively opposed me for my entire political career.”

A desperate Trump then begged, stating, “your favorite President (ME!) is asking all of those who supported Senator John Cornyn to UNITE, and immediately switch your support to Ken Paxton.”

Cornyn has stated he will not help raise money for Paxton’s campaign, telling CNN last month he was a “bad candidate,” and adding, “it’s hard to outrun all the baggage.”

Last month, Rove said Cornyn would have had more chance of beating Talarico than Paxton. 

“If John Cornyn were the nominee, this race would be over,” the former Bush adviser said at the Texas Tribune Festival.

“But when you got a guy who’s got multiple girlfriends, $200,000 worth of improvements in his house from a corrupt business guy for whom he does favors … and now it’s in the court of public opinion. If this were not out there, this would be a normal Republican versus Democrat.”

Paxton’s wife Angela divorced him last year on “biblical grounds.” His latest scandal is a Wall Street Journal report claiming he partied in Dubai with his mistress Tracey Duhon, and two fugitives wanted by the Justice Department.

A new report claims billionaire Elon Musk has thrown $10 million at Paxton’s flailing campaign in an attempt to salvage a victory.

Speaking on CNN’s OutFront on Thursday, former Republican Rep. Charlie Dent called out Trump’s Truth Social post, saying Cornyn was winning races until this primary and “until Donald Trump interceded.”

“The problem with the Paxton race is the candidate,” Dent said. “He’s deeply flawed, unfit on many levels, character issues. That’s the problem, and Donald Trump endorsed him. This is not about John Cornyn. It’s not about Karl Rove. The president is just trying to deflect. And put the blame somewhere else in the event that Paxton loses. It’s as simple as that.”

The White House referred the Daily Beast to Trump’s Truth Social post when asked for further comment.

news.title: Trump 'retribution' looms over red state weighing ouster of MAGA senator: WSJ columnist
news.text:
A conservative editorial board warned voters in one red state that defying President Donald Trump at the ballot box carries a steep price.

Kimberley Strassel, a member of The Wall Street Journal's editorial board, wrote Thursday that Alaska risks losing Trump's favor and possibly facing his retribution if voters oust Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-AK) on November 3.

In her Potomac Watch column, Strassel cast the Senate race between Sullivan and former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola as a choice between continued federal support and what she called "political and economic suicide." She credited Trump with reversing dozens of Biden-era restrictions on drilling, mining and logging in the state and with pushing a long-stalled natural gas pipeline that Sullivan supporters chanted about at a Tuesday rally in Wasilla.

But Strassel also conceded that the windfall hinges on something other than policy. She wrote that the state's gains "come down to" Sullivan's personal relationship with the president, a point she said the senator "can't publicly say." Trump, she noted, harbors a "special dislike" for Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK), who voted to convict him at his 2021 impeachment trial.

"If Mr. Sullivan goes away, so does Alaska's line to the presidency," Strassel wrote.

She went further, questioning whether the Trump administration would keep its current commitments to the state if Peltola joined Murkowski in the Senate. Strassel said new favors would dry up for requests from the two women, and she asked outright whether Trump might punish them. Her answer was "quite possibly."

Strassel also took aim at the state's ranked-choice voting system, which she called "ridiculous," and accused Democrats of gaming it. She pointed to a Peltola donor also named Dan Sullivan who is running as a Republican, a candidate she dubbed "Decoy" Dan, and said GOP organizers were scrambling to teach voters how to fill out their ballots without accidentally electing the Democrat.

Peltola, who represented Alaska in the House from 2022 to 2025, has blamed Trump's economic agenda and Sullivan for high prices in the state and has called the incumbent "corrupt." Strassel dismissed that pitch as a rewrite of recent history.

Strassel wrote that Trump's message to the Wasilla crowd boiled down to a blunt warning. A vote for Peltola, she wrote, would leave the state "toast."

news.title: Europe reckons with a world where Trump is now helping Putin
news.text: European leaders know they can’t stop courting Donald Trump. But as the U.S. president menaces Ukraine and offers Russian an economic lifeline, they are preparing for a world where he effectively sides with Moscow.In the span of a week, Trump has trashed years of energy sanctions on the Kremlin, pressured Kyiv to quit bombing Russian oil refineries and suggested Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy was an illegitimate leader — echoing Moscow’s propaganda. At one point, Ukraine also lost full access to the Elon Musk-owned Starlink system, leaving it hobbled on the battlefield.In response, Zelenskyy let rip. He felt betrayed, he said. He called out Trump in public.

news.title: PM Mark Carney says US is trying to break Canada as Alberta votes on separation path
news.text: CALGARY: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney warned Thursday that the United States is trying to break Canada so it can "own us" as he urged oil-rich Alberta not to begin a process toward separation in Monday's referendum.Monday's vote is not a direct referendum on independence. Alberta, which has the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, will decide whether to remain a province or instruct the government to begin the legal process toward a future referendum on separation."This referendum comes at the worst possible time," Carney told a pro-Canada rally in Calgary. "The world has become more dangerous and divided. Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us."He did not directly mention the U.S. or its President Donald Trump, but has done so in similar past speeches. Carney's warning came amid U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war with Canada and repeated threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state. Carney has argued that Canada needs to become more economically resilient and less dependent on the United States.Carney urged Albertans not to use the vote simply to send Ottawa a message, saying a decisive result could settle the separation question.."Don't be fooled by the idea you can 'send a message' with your vote," Carney said. "This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep division and great uncertainty."Carney makes the case for CanadaCarney, who grew up in Alberta, spent Thursday campaigning in Calgary before addressing the Forever Canadian rally at the BMO Centre. Organizers were also holding a second rally with Carney in Edmonton on Friday.Earlier Thursday, he pointed to the many Albertans who were born or educated elsewhere in Canada and to firefighters who come from across the country to help Alberta during wildfires as examples of the ties binding the province to the rest of Canada.At the rally, Carney also acknowledged the grievances that have fueled alienation in Alberta."The frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real," he said. Carney said that while growing up, Ottawa made Albertans feel "like our resources weren't our own" and that more recently the province was made to feel its energy contributions were "against the tides of history.".A Liberal prime minister finds unlikely supportThe setting is striking for a Liberal prime minister. Alberta has spent decades feuding with Liberal governments in Ottawa, particularly over energy and federal power. But Carney has broken with some of the policies associated with his predecessor, Justin Trudeau, fast-tracked a proposed new oil pipeline to the Pacific and called Canada an energy superpower.Carney pointed to the Pacific Link pipeline as evidence of a changed relationship, saying it would create more than 140,000 jobs, reduce Canada's dependence on the United States and generate revenue for social programs.Tanya Clemens, co-chair of the pro-independence group Let Alberta Decide, acknowledged Carney presents a challenge."He's formidable for sure," Clemens told The Associated Press.Clemens argued, however, that Carney's agreements with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith amount to "pinky promises" that do not resolve long-standing grievances with Ottawa.Keith Wilson, another leader of Let Alberta Decide, rejected Carney's argument that global instability made this the wrong time for the vote.."The worst timing for this, why? I don't understand what's the logic," Wilson said. "Then it's the best time for him to get back to Ottawa."Wilson said Carney should ask Parliament to repeal federal measures that separatists say have hurt Alberta, including authority he says could be used to tax oil exports in retaliation against the United States. He predicted Carney would eventually impose such a tax despite Carney saying he sees no value in using Canadian energy exports as leverage against the U.S."It's one cabinet meeting away," Wilson said. "He's gonna do it. He has to do it."Smith, who called the vote but supports remaining in Canada, cast her ballot Wednesday and said she voted for Alberta to remain in Canada. She has said support for separation remains too high for her liking."Canada can still work," Smith said after voting. "We just need to make some changes."Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University, called Carney's popularity in Alberta "highly unusual" for a Liberal prime minister. He said Carney has also benefited from a "Trump effect," as Trump's trade war and 51st-state threats have rallied Canadians around their leader — even in Alberta..From the political fringe to a provincewide voteThe referendum marks a remarkable rise for a cause long relegated to Alberta's political fringes. After the COVID-19 pandemic and the 2022 Freedom Convoy, activists who had organized against vaccine mandates and other restrictions turned their attention to Alberta independence.The convoy began over vaccine requirements for cross-border truckers but grew into a broader protest against pandemic restrictions, paralyzing downtown Ottawa and blocking major Canada-U.S. border crossings.Clemens said COVID accelerated the movement by teaching people how to organize politically and become more involved in party politics. news.title: Trump banking on ‘swift end’ of Iran war to bring down fuel prices
news.text:
Pezeshkian decries US blockade, insists ‘military force’ will not compel Tehran into submission• Washington weighs using ‘Mother Of All Bombs’ against Iranian energy sites, CNN reports

WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump once again predicted a swift end to the war with Iran, and a sharp drop in oil prices once the conflict concludes, even as Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian warned that military action cannot force them into submission.

“The Iran war will end very soon … Soon, as they want it to end,” Trump told reporters in Montana. “They’ll never have a nuclear weapon, and oil prices will drop like a rock.”

According to Anadolu Agency, Trump also expressed uncertainty over which Ira-nian officials the US was negotiating with.

“They don’t have a navy. They don’t have an air force. Their army is decimated. Their leaders are gone,” Trump said. “I should have probably left their leaders because I don’t know who the hell we’re negotiating with.”

“Iran was the bully of the Middle East,” he said, adding that the country was no longer as powerful as it had been.

Trump also claimed that US strikes had destroyed Iran’s naval fleet and rendered its military aircraft unusable. He said Iran had 159 ships and asserted that none remained operational, while also claiming that its fighter jets had been destroyed on the country’s runways.

‘Iran won’t submit to force’

Meanwhile in Tehran, President Pezeshkian warned that military action cannot force a country into submission, adding that his country “must find a way to strengthen national cohesion and unity”, Al Jazeera reported.

He said that the country was facing its most intense blockade since the 1979 Revolution, accusing the United States of seeking to provoke public protests.

“Over the 48 years since the Revolution, we have never faced such intense blockade, war and difficulties as we are facing now,” Pezeshkian said in a speech broadcast by state television.

He accused Washington of seeking to make life difficult for Iranians to fuel public anger and trigger unrest. Pezeshkian said the US was focusing its efforts on making “the people become upset and face difficulties, and then for social protests to emerge so that they can achieve their sinister objectives”.

‘Mother Of All Bombs’

Meanwhile, the US is considering using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB) bomb — better known by its nickname, the “Mother Of All Bombs” — against Iran if Trump decides to renew combat in the deadlocked war, CNN reported on Thursday.

The military is planning for the potential use of the weapon to target Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites, according to the news outlet, which quoted officials familiar with the matter.

“The MOAB is a massive information operation type weapon that is great for huge area clearance but not much else,” a source familiar with the plans told CNN. “It is definitely not designed as a deep penetration warhead.”

Trump is trying to boost his low approval ratings ahead of November’s midterm elections, with polls showing the unpopular war in Iran and the fuel and other price rises it has caused are hurting his Republican Party.

Diplomatic efforts to end the conflict have been at an impasse since the summer, and Washington has in recent weeks dialled back military operations in favour of economic pressure.

However, officials have raised doubts over the efficacy of the bomb if deployed, particularly its ability to destroy suspected underground nuclear sites in Iran, as well as concerns over possible civilian casualties from such a huge weapon.

Published in Dawn, October 16th, 2026

news.title: US Teen's 'Kill Indians' Plot Was 2 Years In Making, Chose Temple As Target
news.text: A teenager in suburban Chicago, who was arrested before carrying out a mass shooting plot at a Hindu temple last weekend, had been planning the attack for over two years, according to court documents. Prosecutors from the Cook County State's Attorney's Office said the suspect, Alexandros Paporakis, 19, told his coworkers at Taco Bell in Palatine that he "couldn't wait to kill Indian" people. Though the exact intended location of Paporakis' killing plot is still under investigation, police officials in Palatine, Illinois, and FBI investigators said they believe the teenager was planning to attack a large Hindu temple in Aurora, about 40 miles west of Chicago.How A Jammed Gun Stopped The AttackPalatine Police Chief William Nord said a red Acura RDX registered to Paporakis entered a temple parking lot on Sunday around 12:25 pm and left less than 15 minutes later. He was seen alone inside the car around 2 pm near his home in another suburb.Officials did not name the target, but the Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) Temple in Aurora, the area's largest temple, later informed its members of a security threat with a posting on its website. A receptionist at the temple, who did not give her name, told The New York Times on the phone that the temple was indeed the site of the thwarted attack. The American teenager's bloody plans were foiled in time after one of his colleagues reported him to the police. Later, the Mount Prospect and Palatine police departments coordinated to locate and arrest Paporakis while he was leaving his home on Sunday afternoon, the same day prosecutors believe he was planning to execute his plans.The White Supremacist IdeologyDuring searches at his home, which the man had shared with his mother for about a year, police found a rifle, multiple loaded rifle magazines and hundreds of rounds of additional rifle ammunition, a tactical vest containing body armour and a patch displaying imagery associated with white supremacist extremism, officials said. Also found at his home were items with Nazi symbols, including swastikas, and a gas can labelled with an anti-Indian slur. Detectives also examined his electronic communications and a document attributed to Paporakis titled: "Why I Fought: A.K.A.: (Aurora Shooter's Manifesto)", which described Indian, Jewish and African American people as "subhumans" and outlined a plot to kill as many of them as possible, according to a court document. Paporakis faces felony charges of making a terrorist threat and unlawfully possessing a rifle. Prosecutors have said Paporakis, a cashier at a Taco Bell, had texted a co-worker espousing white supremacist views and a plot for a potential mass shooting.Planning Of Special DayHe had told them that Sunday would be the "special day". On Sunday, he reportedly called the co-worker to tell them that his gun had jammed at the scene and that he was fleeing, the documents said.He also reportedly sent a video to his co-worker showing how his gun, an AR-style rifle, had failed to fire and told them that he was trying to fix the weapon so he could "retry" and that "the man that he fired at was 'certainly saved by his God today,'" the court document showed, according to an NYT report. Paporakis had also sent the coworker an eight-page document in which he used racial slurs to describe non-white people and outlined a plot to kill as many of them as possible, according to prosecutors. He also described himself as a white supremacist and a neo-Nazi who fantasised about mass murder.The co-worker called 911, leading to the suspect's arrest.Court documents showed that his colleagues said on Saturday, Paporakis's behaviour had intensified, and that he told one colleague, "He couldn't wait to kill Indian people" and told another co-worker that he was planning "it" at a Hindu temple in Aurora.The Plan Was Two Years in the MakingPaporakis had also reportedly written to a co-worker that he had been planning an attack for two years, and had been looking for a specific location in recent months. Court documents showed that the suspect described his "persona as a working college student as a facade that concealed interior hatefulness and frequent fantasies about mass murder," the NYT report said.Rise Of Anti-India SentimentsPaporakis' arrest added to concerns about a rise in physical and verbal attacks against South Asians, especially Indians, in the United States, under the Donald Trump administration.Earlier this month, a Hindu temple was vandalised outside Cleveland, when an unknown assailant threw a brick through a window. In September, the Department of Homeland Security came under fire after it posted a message on social media with an image of a Sikh man, urging some immigrants to self-deport. The image has since been taken down, but the department called criticism of the post "nonsensical drivel".
news.summary: Palatine Police Chief William Nord said a red Acura RDX registered to Paporakis entered a temple parking lot on Sunday around 12:25 pm and left less than 15 minutes later.

news.title: Self-described 'lawyer' Katie Zacharia defends legal credentials
news.text:
New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia has defended her legal background and justified her truncated inaugural briefing as she navigates a rocky first week as the president's chief spokeswoman.

The Wall Street Journal recently reported Ms Zacharia, introduced by Donald Trump as an attorney, never passed the bar exam in the United States, according to a source with direct knowledge of the matter.

Appointed by US President Donald Trump, Ms Zacharia has described herself as a lawyer during television appearances and on social media, and listed herself as general counsel of a California-based conservative nonprofit.

There is no evidence to suggest that the 41-year-old press secretary has ever passed the bar exam, required to obtain a license to practise law in the United States, after graduating from Pepperdine University with a law degree. 

In her home state of California, it is a misdemeanour to practice law without the appropriate credentials. 

When questioned Thursday, local time, by conservative media outlet Real America's Voice, Ms Zacharia said she had registered to take the bar exam but was then "distracted and overwhelmed" by plans to move to China with her husband.

"I was obviously incredibly distracted and overwhelmed and excited for finally being married to someone who I'd been long distance from for at least a year," Ms Zacharia said.

"We just said, 'Let's take this time, and I'll take the bar and see what happens.' The results are somewhat inconsequential because I knew I wouldn't need the bar in China, and we left shortly thereafter," she said.

On her Linkedin page, Ms Zacharia lists experience at Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing, where she says she worked as an associate for nearly two years.

Ms Zacharia, who has been under scrutiny after an uncomfortable first press briefing on Tuesday, said she consulted several legal experts to ensure that title was accurate when offering legal analysis.

"It's unfortunate that people dub this as some kind of conspiracy or want to put me in a camp. The truth is, I was very careful how I executed this, and I never came across as someone who was an attorney-at-law."

She will not weigh in on legal matters in her White House capacity, Ms Zacharia said.

Zacharia's path to the White House explained 

Ms Zacharia, who previously worked as a communication adviser and who runs Truth Social, said she did not want to be seen as lobbying for the position, left vacant when Karoline Leavitt announced she would depart the administration to spend more time with her family.

She said she monitored the president's social media posts to determine what was top of mind for him, then would go on air to talk about those topics.

"My philosophy is, I'm on TV enough where if he sees me and he likes me, then I will be recruited for the job," she said.

"I do not believe that lobbying for that job would have been successful, and I wanted to work for it. I wanted to audition for it."

Then on October 7, as Zacharia was preparing to take one of her children to a pumpkin patch, she received a phone call from Trump about the press secretary position.

She promptly flew out the next day from her home in California to Washington, met with the president about the job on Friday and formally accepted the position later that day.

Ms Zacharia was later celebrated in a post by Pepperdine University after news of her new position spread. 

Zacharia planned to keep her first press briefing 'short'

In it, she said she did not have time to get fully prepared ahead of her first briefing on Tuesday and that it was always the plan to keep it short because President Donald Trump would field questions from journalists later that morning.

"It was absolutely my goal to keep it short, considering he is his own best spokesperson, and he would love — and does love — gaggling with the media as he goes to Marine One," Ms Zacharia said.

"So I wanted to give ample deference and not barge into his time."

The initial briefing materials were given to Ms Zacharia on Monday evening, then completed on Tuesday at 8am, less than two hours before she would appear before the White House press corps.

She had been up since 3am preparing, Ms Zacharia said.

"I never had a full briefing beforehand, and I went out and I effectuated the briefing," she said.
news.summary: New US press secretary Katie Zacharia defends her legal credentials after a truncated inaugural briefing prompted scrutiny over her suitability for the job.

news.title: Trump says cartels run Mexico, warns of action
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 16 (IANS) US President Donald Trump claimed that drug cartels effectively controlled Mexico and said his administration was intensifying operations against trafficking networks, even as he acknowledged that the Mexican government was unhappy with his assessment. Speaking at a White House Rose Garden lunch honouring first responders, Trump said the United States had achieved major reductions in maritime drug trafficking and was now expanding its efforts against criminal networks operating across the southern border. "We're working with Mexico. But unfortunately, the cartels run Mexico. I tell that to the president of Mexico. She's not happy. She's a great woman, wonderful woman, but the cartels run Mexico," Trump said. Trump said his administration had initially concentrated on stopping drugs entering the United States by sea because maritime trafficking presented particular enforcement challenges. He claimed that the volume of drugs entering through maritime routes had fallen by 97 per cent, although he did not identify the period or data used for the comparison. "We wanted to do the sea and the water first because the water, that's harder to do," he said. Trump described the use of missiles against suspected drug-trafficking vessels, saying the operations had sharply reduced the willingness of traffickers to attempt maritime crossings. "Those missiles come and they hit those boats dead center, and you feel terribly for the people," he said. The President defended the strikes by arguing that drugs transported aboard such vessels caused widespread deaths and devastated American families. He also joked that the operations had discouraged recreational boating and fishing because people feared being mistaken for traffickers. Trump said his administration was preparing to intensify efforts against trafficking routes on land, particularly those associated with Mexican cartels. "We know all the paths, we know where all the bad guys are, the cartels. We know where they live and we're hitting them hard, but it's going to be harder as we go along," he said. He suggested that cartel members had been given an opportunity to surrender, but provided no details of the warning or its implementation. "They know they have a certain period of time to essentially give up. Mexico should be doing it, but honestly, they're not capable of doing it," Trump said. The President separately claimed that the flow of fentanyl across the southern border had declined by 67 per cent. He credited Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Border Patrol personnel with strengthening border security and confronting trafficking organisations. Trump described the border as the most secure in American history and claimed that illegal crossings had been brought down dramatically. He also praised National Border Patrol Council President Paul Perez, who addressed the gathering and credited Trump's leadership with improving national security. Perez said the administration had provided unprecedented support to first responders and border enforcement personnel. The remarks came as the Trump administration continued to place border security, illegal immigration and narcotics trafficking at the centre of its domestic security agenda. The United States and Mexico share an extensive land border and maintain close economic and security ties. Cooperation against organised crime and drug trafficking has long involved law enforcement coordination, intelligence sharing and efforts to disrupt criminal organisations operating across national boundaries.
news.author: IANS News

news.title: ‘I don't trust anybody’: Trump on Netanyahu, Israel's election and potential Iran strikes
news.text: U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that he does not trust anyone in politics when asked whether he trusts Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, while praising their relationship and saying Israelis want him involved in the country's upcoming election. In a wide-ranging interview with Newsmax, Trump also discussed possible new strikes against Iran, including the use of the powerful non-nuclear weapon known as the "mother of all bombs," and sharply criticized Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. In the interview with Newsmax host Rob Finnerty at the White House, Trump was asked directly whether he trusted Netanyahu, with whom he has maintained close political and military ties. "I don't trust anybody, honestly," Trump replied. "I don't trust anybody," he repeated. "In the world of politics, I don't trust anybody." Trump did not indicate that the remarks reflected any specific disagreement with Netanyahu. Instead, he praised their cooperation, particularly during the war against Iran. "Look, I've had a very good relationship with him. We've had good success together." The president was also asked whether he intended to become involved in Israel's October 27 election, in which Netanyahu is seeking another term as prime minister. "Well, they'd like me to be. Yeah, they'd like me to be," Trump said, stopping short of committing to participate in the campaign or endorsing Netanyahu. He went on to boast about his popularity among Israeli voters, claiming that he would receive overwhelming support if he were eligible to run for prime minister. "The people of Israel, they say if I ran for prime minister, I'd get 99% of them," Trump said. The remarks come less than two weeks before Israelis head to the polls, with Netanyahu frequently emphasizing his close relationship with the American president. Trump has so far avoided explicitly endorsing the prime minister ahead of the election. In an interview with Time magazine published October 1, Trump declined to endorse Netanyahu, saying his main priority was helping defend Israel. Trump's comments also came as Washington and Jerusalem continued consultations over Iran, including the possibility of renewed military operations. CNN reported Thursday that the U.S. military had developed new strike plans that could include using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, commonly known as the "mother of all bombs," against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear facilities. Asked about the possibility of deploying the weapon, Trump did not rule it out, but stressed that it was not nuclear. "Well, the mother of all bombs is not nuclear," Trump said. "No, it's not nuclear at all. This is just an extremely large bomb," he added. "It's like a tiny nuclear bomb. The mother of all bombs is one big bomb, but it's not nuclear." The weapon, weighing approximately 21,600 pounds, or 9.8 metric tons, is the largest non-nuclear bomb in the American arsenal. It was used in combat for the first time in 2017, when the U.S. military struck an Islamic State tunnel complex in Afghanistan. According to CNN, the Pentagon's new plans include possible strikes on a heavily fortified Iranian nuclear site known as Pickaxe Mountain. However, military officials have reportedly raised questions about whether the weapon would be effective against deeply buried installations, since it is designed primarily to produce a massive surface blast rather than penetrate thick layers of rock and reinforced concrete. Trump separately emphasized that he did not intend to use nuclear weapons against Iran. He also raised the possibility of future nuclear disarmament talks involving Russia and China, predicting that Beijing could catch up with Washington's nuclear capabilities within five years. Asked why the United States would not simply declare victory and withdraw from Iran after previously claiming that its nuclear program had been destroyed, Trump argued that an early departure could make further military action necessary. "Well, we could. But if we do that within a year we may have to do it again," he said. "We want to make it so that they will never have a nuclear weapon, because if they had it, they would use it, in my opinion, instantaneously." Trump maintained that previous American and Israeli operations had severely damaged Iran's nuclear infrastructure, but suggested that further action could be required against sites believed to remain operational. "Now, we're looking at Pickaxe Mountain. We may have to go there," he said. "We'll take a shot at that one. We'll knock it out fast." Asked whether such an operation could involve deploying American ground troops inside Iran, Trump dismissed the possibility. "No, I don't see that. I don't see that." He also expressed confidence that the war could end soon through negotiations or further military action. "The Iran war will be over very soon. It's going to end very soon," he said. Trump claimed that Tehran had asked Washington and Jerusalem to halt their attacks while negotiations continued. "They've asked us to please stop. And we do, because we're negotiating with them," he said. The president also addressed the continuing war between Russia and Ukraine, directing particularly harsh criticism at Zelensky over Kyiv's renewed attacks on Russian oil refineries. "Zelensky is not a good guy for us to deal with," Trump said, according to an English-language account of the Newsmax interview published by Anadolu Agency. "He doesn't want to settle. He says he wants to settle, but he doesn't. No, I'm not a big fan of Zelensky," he added. Trump accused Ukraine of worsening global energy prices by targeting facilities that produce diesel fuel, which has become particularly expensive amid the broader Middle East conflict. "I think that's a disgrace. There's plenty of other targets," Trump said. "When you shoot at diesel refineries where you make, you know, diesel oil and we need that, and the world needs that, then he's not doing a good service for the world," he added. The comments follow a new dispute between Washington and Kyiv after Trump announced an agreement with Russia intended to increase the availability of diesel on international markets. Zelensky criticized the arrangement and said Ukraine would resume attacks on Russian refineries after accusing Moscow of continuing to strike Ukrainian energy infrastructure despite a proposed pause. Trump also attributed some of the difficulties in reaching a peace agreement to the personal hostility between Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin, arguing that their mutual animosity made negotiations considerably more difficult. The American president again raised the issue of holding new elections in Ukraine. Asked about a proposed pause in fighting to allow a vote, he responded: "I think you need an election." He questioned whether Ukrainian citizens were satisfied with their leadership while Russian missiles continued to strike residential buildings, reinforcing his criticism of Zelensky as the conflict showed little sign of nearing a diplomatic resolution.
news.summary: Asked whether he trusts Netanyahu, Trump says he trusts nobody in politics but praises their partnership; he claims Israel wants him involved in the October 27 election, discusses possible use of the ‘mother of all bombs’ against Iran and criticizes Zelenskyy over strikes on Russian oil refineries

news.title: Frustrated with Trump, voters overwhelmingly want change in Washington, an AP-NORC poll finds
news.text:
WASHINGTON: A strong majority of voters believe that President Donald Trump is falling short at home and abroad, and they want major change in the upcoming midterm elections, according to a new AP-NORC poll that raises serious warning signs for the Republican Party at a critical moment.

The survey from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research, conducted less than four weeks before Election Day, finds that registered voters who identify as Democrats are more enthusiastic than Republican voters about casting a ballot. More voters want Democrats to win control of Congress and have a more negative view of Republicans.

The Democratic advantage is small in some cases, but, taken together, the findings paint a challenging picture for Republicans, who are clinging to control of Congress under the weight of an unpopular war with Iran and surging prices at home.

About 8 in 10 voters overall say the economy or the cost of living is among their top issues for the upcoming election, while about two-thirds say this about health care and the war in Iran. Other issues that are stronger for Trump — like immigration or crime — are lower priorities.

“The world is going backwards. We can barely afford anything,” said Diana Walker, a 65-year-old Democrat from Decatur, Georgia. “Everybody’s down. I don’t care if you’re a Democrat or Republican, we’re all catching hell.”

Democrats are more enthusiastic about voting than Republicans

Less than a month before the final midterm votes are cast, the poll finds that Democratic voters are more motivated to vote.

Overall, about two-thirds of registered voters say it’s “extremely” important to vote in the upcoming election, while about 2 in 10 say it’s “very” important.

But about three-quarters of Democratic voters say that voting in this November’s midterm elections is “extremely” important, compared with roughly 6 in 10 Republicans.

Ryan Longbrake, a 52-year-old Democrat from Columbus, Ohio who works in technology marketing, said he’s especially excited about casting his ballot, and he’s already taken steps to ensure that his wife and two college-age daughters will vote as well.

“I believe that there is change on the horizon and there is an excitement within our party,” he said, pointing to Democrats’ momentum in Ohio’s elections for governor and US Senate. The party is also investing resources in Republican-leaning states, like Iowa and Kansas, where the political environment has put Democratic candidates on friendlier footing.

Republicans have controlled Congress for the past two years, but about half of registered voters now say they’d prefer to see the Democratic Party control the House or the Senate. A smaller percentage, roughly 4 in 10, say they want the Republican Party to control each chamber, while 15 percent are undecided.

The vast majority of voters want change

One thing is crystal clear on the eve of the 2026 midterms: Voters want change.

About half of voters say they want “substantial change,” and roughly 3 in 10 want “complete and total upheaval” in the way the country is run.

Democrats and independents are much likelier than Republicans to want a full overhaul of the country’s direction. But even Republican voters are still looking for something different. Slightly fewer than half, 45 percent, want substantial change, while 13 percent want upheaval.

“I’m kind of tired of sending people there and nothing gets done,” said Krista Kohles, a 70-year-old Republican from near Davey, Nebraska. “Nothing’s changing.”

Trump’s numbers on key issues are weak

Voters are deeply frustrated with Trump and his leadership on the issues they say matter most.

Only about one-third of registered voters overall have a “very” or “somewhat” favorable view of the Republican president, and a similar share approve of his performance as president.

Voters continue to be frustrated by the high cost of living, an issue that Trump vowed to address before winning a second term in the White House.

Nearly two years after his successful election, about 8 in 10 registered voters disapprove of how Trump is handling the cost of living, in line with a September AP-NORC poll. About three-quarters disapprove of his performance on the economy.

Even among Republican voters, only 44 percent approve of Trump’s performance on the cost of living, while 54 percent approve of his leadership on the economy. That’s a sharp contrast with other issues, like crime, on which Republican approval is much higher.

There are cracks in Trump’s Republican base on other issues, too. Just 69 percent of Republican voters support Trump on foreign policy as the war in Iran stretches into its eighth month, despite his promises that it would only last four or five weeks.

DonnaJean Weber, a 72-year-old Republican from Manistee, Michigan, says she will continue to support Republican candidates this fall, but she’s not happy with the state of the economy under Trump’s leadership.

“Everything’s going up,” she said, pointing to the impact of the war with Iran, among other Trump decisions. “I don’t agree with him fully on all of these tariffs, either. It’s making this country look bad.”

The economy and the cost of living are high priorities for voters on both sides of the aisle. The survey found that the vast majority of Republican and Democratic voters say both issues are among the most important for the upcoming election.

Voters aren’t any higher on one of Trump’s potential successors in the next presidential election, Vice President JD Vance: About half have a “somewhat” or “very” negative view of Vance, compared with about one-third who have a positive opinion.

Enthusiasm for the Democrats isn’t overwhelming

Trump’s struggles do not mean that voters are particularly excited about the direction of the Democratic Party.

Overall, about 4 in 10 voters have a “very” or “somewhat” favorable view of the Democrats, while about half view the party unfavorably. That’s roughly similar to views of the GOP, although about 6 in 10 voters view the Republicans unfavorably.

Democratic and Republican voters are equally enthusiastic about their own side, with about 8 in 10 saying they have a favorable view of their own party.

But the critical bloc of voters who identify as independents is much more likely to have a negative view of the Republicans than of the Democrats. About two-thirds of independent voters view the GOP negatively, compared with about 4 in 10 who view Democrats negatively.

Michael Russo, a 51-year-old Texas voter who is not registered with either party, described the state of the country under Republican control as “a nightmare.”

Does he want Republicans to maintain control of Congress? “No, I want them in prison — several of them,” he said. But he’s not thrilled with the Democratic Party, either.

“I’m not confident they’re going to do anything if they get into power,” Russo said.

The margin of sampling error for adults overall is plus or minus 3.9 percentage points, and the margin of error for registered voters is plus or minus 4.2 percentage points.

news.title: Trump, 80, Rewrites Family’s History With Kimberly Guilfoyle
news.text:
President Donald Trump remembered Kimberly Guilfoyle’s marriage to his political foe, Gavin Newsom, but seemed to forget she was also engaged to his son.

Trump, 80, spoke to Newsmax’s Rob Finnerty on Thursday about Guilfoyle, who was unceremoniously given the boot on live television on Tuesday.

Asked whether he would consider pardoning his almost-daughter-in-law if she was prosecuted over her alleged misconduct, Trump said, “I don’t want to think about it.”

“I was disappointed in what I read—I just read some things. I haven’t spoken to her,” the president said.

He continued, “I’ve known her over the years; I’ve known her for many years. She was married to Gavin ‘Newscum,’ and, um, I’ve known her for years. Not that well, but I’ve known her.”

The president failed to mention that his son, Donald Trump Jr., had been engaged to Guilfoyle for roughly four years.

“And actually, the interesting thing is, she was the toast of the town over in Greece,” Trump continued. “She was doing a very good job as the, you know, ambassador to Greece. So I’m disappointed.”

Despite trying to distance himself from his failed diplomat, Trump has been much closer to Guilfoyle than he has let on.

As recently as March, Trump described Guilfoyle as “a person I know very, very well.”

“She’s an inspiration to a lot of people, especially if you happen to be Greek,” he said during a Greek Independence Day celebration at the White House. “Kimberly Guilfoyle has been my friend for a long time. I love calling her ‘Kimber-lay.’”

He even attended her 54th birthday party in 2023, appearing alongside her and his son in a photo carousel Guilfoyle shared on Instagram.

However, in the wake of her misconduct allegations, which include her allegedly soliciting $100,000 in exchange for political favors, Trump has tried to downplay the extent of their relationship.

“She was not a member of my family,” he told reporters outside the White House on Tuesday. “She, I guess, dated my son a long time ago.”

Guilfoyle and Donald Jr. started dating in 2018 and were engaged in 2020. The couple called off their engagement in 2024. 

Just over a year later, Donald Jr. got engaged to socialite Bettina Anderson, and the two wed in May of this year. The president did not attend his son’s ceremony.

Beyond being scrubbed from the Trump family tree, her biography was erased from the U.S. Embassy in Greece’s website. Her successor, Josh Huck, now fills the page.

Trump, 80, spoke to Newsmax’s Rob Finnerty on Thursday about Guilfoyle, who was unceremoniously given the boot on live television on Tuesday.

Asked whether he would consider pardoning his almost-daughter-in-law if she was prosecuted over her alleged misconduct, Trump said, “I don’t want to think about it.”

news.title: Ilhan Omar’s husband snaps over allegations she fled US after DC home was raided by feds
news.text:
While Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., has not been seen publicly since federal agents raided her Washington, D.C., residence on Monday, her political consultant husband was once again spotted emerging from their shared rental home this week.

Tim Mynett was seen Wednesday stepping out in the neighborhood to walk their Golden Labrador Retriever dog Teddy, a second time later that same day to take out the trash and a third time to walk out his wife’s staffer.

“There are rumors that the congresswoman left the country, is that true?” Mynett was asked while on an evening walk with Teddy.

“You guys are annoying the hell out of all the neighbors around here, man,” he told Fox News Digital when approached about the developments this week, including President Donald Trump weighing in on the saga.

One of Omar’s congressional staffers was captured the same day bringing into the couple’s home two large bags from fast food chain Burger King. Security escorted her to the door and staked out in front of the house after she entered with the meal.

Rumors swirled that Omar fled from the country following the raid carried out by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) as part of a criminal fraud investigation looking into the Somali-born congresswoman’s immigration paperwork, as first reported by Fox News Digital.

Omar’s cellphone and passport were reportedly seized by federal authorities during the search.

The congresswoman’s staff helped to get her birth year adjusted from 1981 to 1982 in the Minnesota Legislative Reference Library, according to reporters. Omar gained citizenship automatically through her father’s naturalization since she was reportedly 17 years old at the time. If Omar was born in 1981, she would have been 18 years old, meaning the validity of her citizenship could be threatened because she was no longer a minor.

The altered birthdate was published during her entire time serving in Minnesota’s House and for months into her time serving in Congress.

When asked about the federal investigation earlier this week, Mynett told Fox News Digital he has “no concerns” about what federal authorities will find on his wife while investigating her immigration pathway.

“My wife came here when she was 12 years old as a child war refugee,” Mynett said. “No concerns.”

His comments to Fox News Digital come after Omar’s relatives were reportedly issued subpoenas as part of HSI’s investigation into the congresswoman’s immigration paperwork. At least two of Omar’s relatives were subpoenaed, one of which is reportedly Omar’s sister, Sahra Noor.

Fox News Digital asked Mynett about President Donald Trump publicly questioning Omar’s net worth by alleging on Truth Social that her accountant may have reported fraudulent money when her previous financial disclosure listed the couple’s shared net worth as high as $30 million.

“Why did Ilhan Omar report a Net Worth of up to 30 Million Dollars just a short time ago, and then immediately say, “Oh, I made a mistake! It’s really $100,000.” Could it be that her highly paid accountant actually reported the money that was stolen from her fraudulent activities in Minnesota? Would something like that be possible? Do you think the accountant actually gave the right number the first time, 30 Million Dollars, and then she was forced to disavow because she never would have been able to report where that much money came from? She must have freaked out when she saw that money!” Trump posted to Truth Social on Tuesday.

“Where did her house come from, where did her cars come from, and what about her lovely place in Washington, D.C.? I didn’t know that Congressmen and women made that kind of money, but I do know her husband, according to information and belief, makes almost nothing, so it couldn’t have come from him. How many people did she illegally bring into our Country from Somalia? America wants answers, and we want them, NOW!”

Mynett is at the center of yet another investigation into Omar — this time looking into her finances.

Following Monday’s HSI raid, U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said Tuesday that her office is also investigating Omar’s financial disclosures about reporting of her and Mynett’s shared net worth.

Scrutiny of Omar’s finances intensified after her 2024 congressional financial disclosure listed business interests associated with Mynett valued between $6 million and $30 million. Omar’s office subsequently said the figures were incorrect and amended the filing.

The largest change in the documents was from Mynett’s assets. His reported ownership interests in both his winery and venture capital advisory firm, which were previously valued in the millions of dollars, are listed with no value now.

In Omar’s 2024 financial disclosure records, Mynett’s share in his winery was valued between $1 million and $5 million, and his share at the venture capital advisory firm was valued between $5 million and $25 million. Now, his equity interests are both listed at $0.

Omar’s office previously told Fox News Digital that Mynett has partners in both businesses and said the earlier disclosure mistakenly reflected the businesses’ total equity rather than his ownership interest. The office also said the original filing listed assets without accounting for liabilities.

Officials noted that the investigation into Omar’s financial disclosures is unrelated to the raid on her home.
news.summary: Tim Mynett, husband of Rep. Ilhan Omar, dismissed rumors that she fled the US after federal agents raided her home in an immigration fraud probe.
news.author: Fox News

news.title: Disgusting And Despicable: Vance Warns Against Selling White House Access
news.text: Michigan: US Vice President JD Vance on Thursday (local time) said anyone found selling access to the White House should face consequences, responding to questions about allegations involving former US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle and potential conflicts of interest in President Donald Trump's administration, CBS News reported."First of all, if somebody's selling access to the White House, that's disgusting and despicable, and they should suffer consequences," Vance told CBS News.Speaking with 'CBS Evening News' anchor Tony Dokoupil during a town hall in Michigan, scheduled to air on Saturday, Vance said allegations should be assessed based on evidence."I want to make those judgments based on the facts and not based on a random news media report that I read," he said.Dokoupil raised reports concerning Trump's cryptocurrency earnings and Guilfoyle's departure from her diplomatic post following allegations that she had asked a man seeking assistance from the Trump administration to wire her USD 100,000.Asked whether the administration would comply with congressional subpoenas if Democrats won control of the House of Representatives or the Senate in the midterm elections, Vance said, "Of course I will. Look, I mean, we follow the law."Earlier on Tuesday, Guilfoyle confirmed that she was leaving her post as US Ambassador to Greece after the White House asked her to resign.In a post on X, she denied the allegations and said, "I also want to address the recent allegations against me. These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity."White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia said Guilfoyle had been asked to leave her post. "She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well," Zacharia said.Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Trump distanced himself from Guilfoyle, saying she had previously dated his eldest son, Donald Trump Jr."She wasn't a member of my family. She, I guess, dated my son a long time ago," Trump said, according to Fox News. He added, "She was doing a good job, but we didn't like what we were reading."The Wall Street Journal reported that Guilfoyle had asked Trump donor Eric Deters to pay a USD 100,000 American Express bill shortly before her Senate confirmation hearing in July 2025. Deters said he did not make the payment, while Guilfoyle's attorney, Jesse Binnall, disputed the authenticity of the messages cited in the report.Separately, financial disclosures released by the US Office of Government Ethics showed that Trump reported more than USD 1.4 billion in income from his family's cryptocurrency ventures in 2025, including more than USD 500 million from World Liberty Financial and USD 635 million from the sale of his $TRUMP meme coins.The reports have raised questions about potential conflicts of interest involving the President's business interests and his public office. Trump has denied any conflicts of interest.

news.title: Trump Calls Ukraine’s Strikes on Russian Oil Refineries a ‘Disgrace’
news.text:
US President Donald Trump called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries a “disgrace” and accused Kyiv of driving up global energy prices, even as Moscow continued attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

“Well, I think that’s a disgrace,” Trump told Newsmax in an interview published Thursday, Oct. 15, when asked about Ukraine’s decision to resume attacks on Russian refineries.

However, energy analysts say Trump’s deal to resume Russian diesel exports is unlikely to significantly lower fuel prices, as the main driver of the global price surge has been the US–Israel war with Iran, which has disrupted oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump also renewed his criticism of President Volodymyr Zelensky, portraying him as a greater obstacle to ending Russia’s war than Russian President Vladimir Putin.

“It should end soon. I think they actually both would like to see it end,” Trump said.

“But I think I find Zelensky to be more difficult to deal with than Putin.”

His remarks came after Zelensky announced that Ukraine would no longer observe a pause in strikes against Russian refineries, citing Moscow’s continued attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities despite a ceasefire announced by Trump.

“The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” Zelensky told the Financial Times in an interview published Thursday.

Kyiv had temporarily suspended refinery attacks following Washington’s request, but Russian forces continued launching missiles and drones against Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure, leaving hundreds of thousands without electricity.

On Thursday, Ukraine struck an oil refinery in Russia’s Ryazan region, triggering a fire at the facility approximately 300 kilometers southeast of Moscow.

The dispute has deepened tensions between Kyiv and Washington following Trump’s agreement with Putin to ease restrictions on Russian diesel, a move Zelensky has criticized for providing economic relief to Moscow while it continues its invasion.

In Thursday, Zelensky met NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Brussels and held talks with European leaders ahead of Friday’s EU summit, seeking continued military and political support for Ukraine.

Zelensky has argued that stopping attacks on Russian refineries must be matched by an end to Moscow’s strikes on Ukraine’s electricity grid, rather than a one-sided restriction on Kyiv’s ability to fight back.

“Don’t attack us. Don’t kill our children. We will stop attack your diesel,” Zelensky said in an Oct. 11 interview with ABC News, outlining Ukraine’s position on a reciprocal energy ceasefire.
news.summary: Trump condemned Ukraine’s resumption of attacks on Russian refineries, blaming Kyiv for rising energy prices and describing Zelensky as more difficult to negotiate with than Putin.
news.author: Kyiv Post

news.title: Trump ‘plainly guilty’ in case his handpicked judge derailed: ex-prosecutor
news.text:
A former federal prosecutor says President Donald Trump would likely have been convicted if not for one person he picked himself.

Harry Litman, host of "Talking Feds," said in a Thursday episode that the Mar-a-Lago classified documents case was "totally righteous, totally strong" and, "but for Cannon and the happenstance of the election," would have led to a conviction. He was referring to U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon, whom Trump appointed during his first term.

"The Mar-a-Lago purloining of documents and obstructing the department was a layup on the evidence," Litman said. "So he's so plainly guilty."

Litman's comments came as the 11th Circuit Court of Appeals granted Trump's request to postpone oral argument, previously set for November 2, in the fight over Volume II of special counsel Jack Smith's report. Cannon has kept that volume, which covers the documents case, under wraps for more than a year, and First Amendment groups, including the Knight First Amendment Institute, have asked the appeals court to force its release.

Trump's lawyers first pointed to scheduling conflicts and to concerns involving his former co-defendants Walt Nauta and Carlos De Oliveira, whose cases have been dismissed. They later cited a motion from FBI agents seeking guidance from Cannon after being called before a grand jury, a motion Litman noted Cannon had already struck from the record.

Litman, who said he has argued "a lot of appeals, including for the government," said reasons like those normally "wouldn't cut it, but this case is not normal."

He accused Cannon of "bending over backwards, doing backward cartwheels in order to serve the interests of Donald Trump," and said the chief judge of her district had told her not to take the case in the first place.

The appeals court's order said argument would be set at a time convenient to the panel and the attorneys. "That is music to his ears," Litman said. "That's just an indefinite delay, among other things, past when the midterms play out."

Litman argued the report would undercut Trump's long-running attacks on Smith's prosecutions. "I think that report, when it comes out, is going to be very damning and really rebut very forcefully the tired and empty charges of weaponization," he said.

"But it ain't going to be super soon," he added.

news.title: Brent steady as US weighs easing curbs on global ‘shadow fleet’
news.text:
HOUSTON: Brent crude was little changed on Thursday as investors weighed possible US steps to ease restrictions on the world’s “shadow fleet” of tankers, while conflict in the Middle East kept a geopolitical risk premium in the market.

The international benchmark settled down 14 cents, or 0.13 percent, at USD105.92 a barrel.

US West Texas Intermediate crude futures settled up USD2.88, or 3.03 percent, to USD97.97 a barrel, after a large US crude stock draw helped support prices.

The shadow fleet discussions are happening days after President Donald Trump temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel fuel to ease a surge in prices globally. The new talks centre on Washington potentially allowing “legal oil” to flow on previously sanctioned vessels, a US official said.

The Department of Energy said any move to relieve sanctions on the shadow fleet would not help Russia move oil or oil products. The Treasury Department referred questions to the Department of Energy.

US crude stocks and distillate inventories fell while gasoline inventories rose last week, the Energy Information Administration said on Thursday.

Crude inventories fell by 8.6 million barrels to 415.6 million barrels in the week ended October 9, the EIA said, compared with analysts’ expectations in a Reuters poll for a 288,000-barrel draw.

SHIP ATTACKS SUSTAIN OIL RISK PREMIUM

Escalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis and renewed attacks on ships in the region supported prices.

A container ship and a dry bulk carrier both sank near the Strait of Hormuz after being hit by projectiles in separate incidents, maritime officials said on Wednesday.

Attacks around the waterway have surged over the past 10 days, with Iran saying it was stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions introduced last month.

“The ongoing conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis is keeping a geopolitical premium in oil markets, but energy infrastructure has not been attacked in the last several days,” MUFG analysts said in a note.

Houthis fired missiles at the presidential palace complex in the southern city of Aden on Thursday, killing two guards, while the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen detailed dozens of attacks on Saudi infrastructure in the escalating conflict.

Ukraine resumed its attacks on Russian refineries with a strike on a plant in the Ryazan region, after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy voiced anger at a “dangerous” withdrawal of US intelligence.

The International Energy Agency agreed on Thursday to release over 20 million barrels of diesel to the market as soon as possible and any oil remaining from a record emergency reserves release pledged in March to boost supply and cool soaring prices.

In March, countries had pledged to release more than 400 million barrels of crude and oil products as prices soared.

Spain will release 4.4 million barrels from strategic reserves in October, an Energy Ministry official said on Thursday.
