news.title: Zelenskyy’s worst nightmare is here: Ukraine runs out of Patriot missiles
news.text: Ukraine has run out of missiles for its US-made Patriot air defence systems, leaving it vulnerable to Russian ballistic missile attacks, CNN reported citing a source familiar with the situation.The shortage comes amid mounting pressure on US weapons stocks, tensions between Washington and Kyiv over attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, and uncertainty over continued American military support.According to CNN, Ukraine's shortage of Patriot interceptors left almost all Russian ballistic missiles in the latest overnight attack unintercepted.The strikes hit three power plants in Kyiv and targeted energy infrastructure in Kharkiv, killing four people and injuring 25 in the Ukrainian capital. The shortage has raised concerns about Ukraine's ability to protect critical infrastructure as Russia continues its attacks on the country's energy network.The interceptors are expensive and in short supply globally, with countries depleting their stockpiles or seeking to replenish their air defence systems amid the ongoing war involving Iran. The shortage has intensified concerns over Washington's ability to meet Ukraine's requirements while addressing its own military needs and those of its allies.The shortage has coincided with a sharp deterioration in relations between US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, following Washington's controversial deal to import Russian diesel and Trump's push for an energy ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv.Zelenskyy has accused Russia of continuing attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure despite Kyiv temporarily halting strikes on Russian oil facilities in response to the proposal.The dispute has extended beyond weapons supplies to US intelligence and satellite communications. Ukrainian officials told CNN they had not received the early-warning alerts about Russian ballistic missile launches that had previously helped authorities warn civilians to seek shelter.Separately, restrictions affecting Starlink connectivity used by Ukrainian military drones disrupted some offensive and defensive operations. Elon Musk said decisions on military-grade Starshield access rest with the US government, highlighting Kyiv's dependence on American-controlled technology.
news.summary: Ukraine's shortage of Patriot air defence missiles has left it exposed to Russian missile attacks and critical infrastructure damage. Recent attacks have targeted power plants in Kyiv and Kharkiv, resulting in casualties. Relations between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the US government have soured amid disputes over energy and military support. Additionally, limitations on Starlink connectivity have disrupted military operations in Ukraine.
news.author: Aryan Singh

news.title: Gavin Newsom and Arnold Schwarzenegger couldn’t have looked happier slapping backs — but it’s Californians who suffer
news.text:
Gavin Newsom and Arnold Schwarzenegger bonded this week as they celebrated the 20th anniversary of AB 32, California’s cap-and-trade — excuse us, cap-and-invest — program.

AB 32 has raised the price of fuel in California by 5%, or 26 cents per gallon at current prices. Working Californians suffer most.

Meanwhile, AB 32 has done nothing to help the climate. In fact, California’s wildfires have emitted so much carbon dioxide that they have canceled out decades of emissions reductions through AB 32 and other measures.

And California is a negligible factor in global climate anyway, despite its large economy.

So AB 32 is a failure. A big one.

It is said that failure is an orphan, while success has many fathers. But not this time.

Download The California Post App, follow us on social, and subscribe to our newsletters 

These two fathers of California’s green agenda, Newsom and Schwarzenegger, seem eager to claim credit for a policy that continues to make life in the state unaffordable. 

The question is why. 

One answer is that Newsom’s presidential ambitions are becoming more urgent as the nation moves closer to the midterm election.

Sharing a stage with Schwarzenegger is a way for him to burnish his bipartisan credentials — even though he has governed from the left.

For Schwarzenegger, appearing alongside Newsom is a way to stay relevant.

Few Californians have fond memories of Schwarzenegger’s terms in office. 

He was elected on a promise of reform, but turned and ran the moment the unions put up a fight. 

He left office with the state in fiscal disarray, and his personal reputation in tatters.

He emerged to shout insults at Donald Trump, who won the presidency anyway.

Schwarzenegger, in other words, is a political failure.

But every year or two, the sitting governor invites him to a climate event.

And suddenly, he’s a hero again, saving the planet.

And that points to the real reason Newsom and Schwarzenegger are celebrating AB 32.

Cap-and-trade is the ultimate virtue signal. It is a way to look like you are doing something good for the world, even though, at best, you aren’t doing anything at all.

The climate emperor has no clothes.

But no one will state the obvious, as long as both of them — the Republican who launched it, the Democrat who extended it — agree to keep pretending. 

So they united to blow out the proverbial candles on AB 32’s birthday cake.

Carbon-free candles, we presume.
news.summary: Gavin Newsom and Arnold Schwarzenegger bonded this week as they celebrated the 20th anniversary of AB 32, California’s cap-and-trade — excuse us, cap-and-invest — program.

news.title: Trump hits back at Zelensky and brands him 'not a good guy' in blistering attack
news.text: Donald Trump has hit out at Volodymyr Zelenskyy branding him "not a good guy" in a new blistering attack. It comes just days after the pair fell out after the Ukrainian leader branded a US deal to buy Russian diesel a “gift” to Russian President Vladimir Putin. In an interview with Newsmax Trump addresses the Russia - Ukraine war, he said: "Zelenskyy is not a good guy for us to deal with." Trump was then asked by the presenter: "Have you lost faith in him?" To which Trump replied: "Well, I think they're going to end up with a settlement of some kind, they're not going to do it with him, he doesn't want to settle. He says he wants to settle but he doesnt. No I'm not a big fan of Zelenskyy they've destroyed that country." Trump went on to say: "Putin hates Zelenskyy and Zelenskyy hates Putin and when you have that kind of hatred it's very hard to get something settled; but that's a war that should have never started." Asked if the war will end before he leaves office Trump said: " It should end soon I think they actually both would like to see it end. But I think I find Zelenskyy more difficult to deal with than Putin." news.title: Katie Zacharia’s Posts Come Back to Bite Her
news.text:
White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia failed the bar exam yet still shared at least 15 social posts calling her an “attorney.”

Zacharia, 41, failed the exam at Pepperdine University in 2011, after graduating from law school there, The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday, after questions were raised about her credentials. Zacharia told The New York Times that same day that Pepperdine’s president had advised her not to use the terms “attorney” or “esquire” during her cable news appearances, but “lawyer” would be fine.

“The truth is, is I was very careful how I executed this, and I never came across as someone who was an attorney at law,” Zacharia similarly told Real America’s Voice.

But Zacharia had no problem over the past two years sharing social media posts labeling her an “attorney,” CNN reports. On X and Truth Social from April 2025 until last month, Zacharia amplified at least 15 Fox News stories and One America News segments that referred to her as such.

In a now-deleted April 26, 2025 post on X, Zacharia shared the following Fox News headline: “Only Democrats don’t want proof of citizenship in US elections, attorney says.” That same headline showed up on her Truth Social account six times that day, and once more on May 14, according to CNN.

Other posts include one on Truth Social on August 23, 2025. “While @realDonaldTrump is brokering peace deals, Newsom is ‘yammering on’ and not working, says attorney,” she wrote, copying the title of a Fox News story.

In May, June and September of this year, Zacharia shared six posts by One America News in which she was called an “attorney.”

The word “attorney” has also come out of Zacharia’s own mouth. In an Aug. 31 Fox News appearance discussing the prosecution of the accused killer of Charlie Kirk, she said, “As a lawyer, the procedural steps are absolutely critical to ensure that they get this right.”

The Fox chyron then also listed the 41-year-old as an “attorney.” The network did the same same on other occasions.

A source familiar with Zacharia’s thinking told CNN that sharing the posts about her media appearances wasn’t meant to show that she approved of that use of the “attorney” title.

The White House has publicly been supportive of Zacharia.

Communications Director Steven Cheung has said that Zacharia “is a fabulous and wonderful addition to the team.” 

“She is uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as Press Secretary,” he added.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

After failing the bar, Zacharia joined the Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing as an associate on its international practice team. She was told a law license wasn’t required for her to give legal analysis, the Journal reported.

“I practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials,” Zacharia said in a statement earlier this week, amid questions about whether she was an attorney, as Donald Trump said on Truth Social while announcing her for the role.

The controversy has spurred the ethics watchdog group Campaign for Accountability to call for an investigation by the California state bar into whether Zacharia broke the law. In California, it is a misdemeanor to falsely represent oneself as a practicing lawyer, with a punishment of up to a year in jail or a fine no more than $1,000, or both.

Zacharia’s bar failure aside, many Pepperdine alumni have objected to her new position.

“As a Pepperdine graduate, I’m ashamed to see my alma mater celebrating this,” Instagram user “Waldmansheeranfamily” wrote in response to a glowing post about Zacharia from the school and Dean Paul Caron. “To me, this administration represents the exact opposite of everything Pepperdine taught us to stand for. Deeply disappointing.”

That comment was “liked” 587 times as of publication.

news.title: ASIA WATCH: Nepal urges global climate action after devastating Himalayan floods
news.text:
Prime Minister Balendra Shah, a former rapper who took office in March, appealed for international solidarity at the U.N. General Assembly in September, warning that Nepal was paying a heavy price for climate change despite contributing little to global greenhouse gas emissions.

The disaster has highlighted growing concerns over the threat posed by melting glaciers, while rising sea levels are also putting vulnerable island nations at risk, prompting aid officials to stress the need for greater international cooperation.

"Nepal contributes less than 0.1 percent of global greenhouse-gas emissions. We did not create this crisis. Yet we are paying a colossal price for it," Shah told world leaders in New York on Sept. 24.

Shah attended the gathering himself following the disaster, although Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal had originally been scheduled to represent Nepal.

Describing the devastating floods as what many had called a "Himalayan tsunami," Shah urged world leaders to take concrete action rather than simply make promises.

"Climate justice cannot just remain a beautiful phrase in a United Nations document," he said.

His appeal comes as the world's biggest greenhouse gas emitters face mounting pressure to do more to tackle climate change.

China accounted for 29.2 percent of global emissions in 2024, while the combined share of China, the United States and India reached 48.5 percent.

U.S. President Donald Trump's administration formally repealed most of the greenhouse gas emission standards introduced for fossil fuel-fired power plants, marking a further rollback of U.S. climate regulations.

One expert has warned that the threat of similar disasters is increasing in mountainous countries as global warming accelerates the melting of snow and ice.

Rijan Bhakta Kayastha, a professor of Kathmandu University, who studied glaciers at Nagoya University's graduate school in Japan, said observations showed that temperatures in the higher reaches of the Himalayas were rising faster than the national average.

This was accelerating the melting of snow and ice, he said, warning that other mountainous countries also faced a growing risk of disasters.

The effects of global warming are not confined to mountain regions. Rising sea levels are also threatening low-lying island nations, including Tuvalu and Vanuatu, raising fears that parts of their territory could eventually be submerged.

Marshall Islands President Hilda Heine voiced similar concerns at the United Nations, saying that continued investment in fossil fuels was "not only immoral but irrational."

In Nepal, efforts are underway to strengthen measures to prevent further disasters, with international aid officials calling for greater investment in preparedness.

Kyoko Yokosuka, the U.N. Development Programme's resident representative in Nepal, who is involved in relief efforts following the floods, said satellite-based glacier monitoring, stronger early warning systems and information sharing with neighboring countries were essential to reducing the risks.

She also stressed the importance of investing in disaster prevention before calamities strike, rather than relying solely on relief efforts afterward.

The Nepalese government and the UNDP launched an initiative this year to lower water levels at four glacial lakes in the country by constructing artificial drainage channels, part of efforts to reduce the danger of sudden flooding.

For those who have already lost their homes, however, the focus is on whether the international community will heed Nepal's warning.

Min Kumar Khatiwada, 54, whose home in Devighat in central Nepal was damaged by the floods, forcing him to move elsewhere, said he hoped Shah's appeal would lead to meaningful action.

"The prime minister has raised an important issue," he said after listening to the speech. "I hope people around the world will listen to Nepal's message and take steps to address the problem."
news.summary:
Nepal is stepping up calls for major greenhouse gas emitters to take action against climate change after devastating floods trigge

news.title: What we know about the investigation into Trump critic Ilhan Omar and the raid on her home
news.text:
More details have emerged about a pre-dawn raid earlier this week on the house of an outspoken critic of US President Donald Trump.

It is understood that the Trump administration is aiming to build a case to strip Minnesota representative Ilhan Omar of her US citizenship, according to sources familiar with the case.

Mr Trump has denied being involved in the raids, while ratcheting up insults against Ms Omar's origins.

Ms Omar, born in Somalia, became a naturalised US citizen in 2000.

Here's how the case could evolve.

What do we know about the investigation so far?

Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), carried out a search on Ms Omar's Washington DC home on Monday, local time.

HSI agents could be seen removing boxes labelled "Seized Property Evidence".

It is now understood the seized items included Ms Omar's phone and that more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas have been issued.

These subpoenas extended to some of Ms Omar's relatives.

US media reported the HSI probe is focused on how Ms Omar obtained her citizenship, and whether her father lied about her age when obtaining citizenship.

The sealed warrant listed conspiracy, false statements on immigration paperwork and immigration fraud as potential crimes, one person familiar with the case told Reuters.

The US Attorney's office is investigating Ms Omar's financial disclosures alongside the immigration probe, US Attorney Jeanine Pirro told Fox News.

"There are several investigations going on" Ms Pirro said.

Ms Omar's finances have previously been scrutinised because her husband, Timothy Mynett, owns stakes in two companies.

Ms Omar's office denied wrongdoing and labelled the raid an "unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies."

The raid occurred during Ms Omar's final weeks of a re-election bid, as a Democrat frequently targeted by Mr Trump and a member of the "squad", a group of young congresswomen of colour including Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

"No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies," her office said on X.

Mr Trump denied knowledge of the investigation, but later emphasised her Somali origins at an Ohio rally.

"She's telling us about the Constitution, and she comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet," Mr Trump said, as the crowd shouted, "deport".

How did Ilhan Omar become a citizen?

Ms Omar and her family fled Somalia as refugees after the country descended into civil war.

They came to the US in 1995.

She became eligible for citizenship in 2000.

US media reports the investigation is determining whether her father lied about her age on the application, writing she was 17 rather than 18.

If Ms Omar was 18, she would be responsible for her own immigration process.

Ms Omar's campaign previously told AP she and others cannot get birth certificates because Somalia's infrastructure collapsed during the civil war.

Since 2016, she has also faced speculation she married her brother.

No proof emerged to support these claims, despite Mr Trump repeating them.

In 2018, The Minneapolis Star Tribune reported Ms Omar showed a reporter phone images of documents from her family's entry into the US.

They listed her father and siblings in birth order, with Ms Omar listed as the youngest of seven children.

Her first husband's name, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, did not appear in the documents.

According to the couple's marriage certificate, he is also three years younger than Ms Omar, whose mother died when she was two years old.

The Obama administration declined to investigate these claims at the time.

The state of deportation in the US

The Homeland Security threat of deportation is real to many Somali-Americans.

In Ms Omar's case, this would occur as denaturalisation, in which citizenship is revoked, though the Justice Department must file a lawsuit proving the person lied in a material way during their application.

Last week, Attorney General Todd Blanche boasted of the "largest denaturalisation effort in modern history" after the Justice Department filed 40 cases.

In Mr Trump's second term, the justice department has filed at least 164 denaturalisation cases.

The Trump administration has cracked down on naturalisation, with denial applications more than doubling between May 2024 and May 2026, according to the National Foundation for American Policy.

The American Civil Liberties Union accused the administration of "embarking on the largest de-legalisation campaign our nation has seen in generations" and of targeting " Black and Brown citizens".

The Trump administration previously terminated Temporary Protected Status for Somalis, though a court challenge is underway.
news.summary: Minnesota democrat Ilhan Omar has been a US citizen since 2000. According to US media reports, the latest raids on her home may be attempting to undo that.

news.title: More humiliation for new press secretary Katie Zacharia as Trump's team trade 'embarrassing' details from her past... and one insider reveals real reason she was hired: MARK HALPERIN
news.text:
By any reasonable assessment, President Donald Trump's new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia has gotten off to a rocky start.

The scale of her debut faceplant is now being unfavorably compared to Anthony Scaramucci's 11-day stint as Trump's White House communications director and Geraldo Rivera's opening of Al Capone's vault.

But senior members of President Trump's team tell me that they believe the biggest threat to Zacharia's survival in the job is not her maiden turn at the podium, nor the controversy over her seemingly flagrant misrepresentation of her legal credentials.

Rather, it is the unknowns in her background – a past that appears to have not been thoroughly checked out before she took on Washington's highest profile positions – that are causing the most concern.

Zacharia, a 42-year-old mother of four, arrived at the James S Brady Press Briefing Room podium seeming like a deer that had been assured shortly before encountering headlights that speeding semis are perfectly harmless.

The degree to which she appeared unprepared, perhaps unqualified, to brief the nation on Tuesday morning was immediately apparent to journalists in the room and, I'm told, White House staff watching – through the fingers of hands pressed to faces – behind the scenes.

Her initial outing lasted about 14 minutes, half spent stiltedly reading from a script and the other half spent taking questions from just three reporters. But putting aside her pilloried podium performance for a moment, Zacharia was standing on a tinderbox.

Introduced as 'an attorney' by the President, she was set upon by reporters as she stood behind Trump on their way to boarding Air Force One. Asked where she passed the bar exam, she replied: 'When I moved to China.'

Zacharia later told The New York Times that she misheard the question and thought she was being asked where she went after law school.

Indeed, she moved to China with her husband after graduating with a law degree from Pepperdine University in 2011.

The Wall Street Journal reports that Zacharia took the California bar examination after law school and failed. Reuters could find no record of her admission to the bar in any state or Washington, DC, even though Zacharia has identified herself as 'general counsel' for a US company on LInkedIn and as a lawyer in multiple TV interviews.

There's certainly nuance here that deserves inclusion and exploration. But it does not answer the more obvious question: Didn't anyone in the White House bother to check on her credentials, her work history, and the particulars of her long stint in China with her husband?

Zacharia also appears to have received a hyper-abbreviated orientation.

Named by Trump on a Friday, she was in front of the media on Tuesday. A long weekend was never going to turn a cable-news commentator into a capable White House press secretary, but watching her debut, one wonders whether those 72-hours were used particularly well.

Also, why the rush? The administration presumably could have survived a few more days without that briefing. And another week spent learning the machinery, meeting reporters and establishing relationships might have helped her, calmed nerves and generated a few pieces of friendly press to pave the way for her first appearance.

The Daily Mail reported that Trump selected Zacharia without consulting White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. That would help explain why some members of Wiles's team have not exactly resembled a welcoming committee.

The speed and savagery by which Zacharia's new colleagues began anonymously trashing her to any reporter with a phone was remarkable, even for a Trump White House.

While the President pronounced her performance 'very good,' those watching without the obligation of having hired her reached other conclusions.

Both things can, of course, be true: Hostile colleagues and Zacharia's apparent inadequacies.

The comparison that comes to mind is former Alaska Governor Sarah Palin taking Republican presidential nominee John McCain's invitation to join his ticket: an ambitious politico accepting an extraordinary promotion for which she was unready, with practically no runway to get ready.

There are occasions when the smartest answer to a powerful person offering you a dream job is: Thank you, but no. Zacharia's failure to recognize such a moment tells us something about her judgment.

While she did not need enemies or skeptics to have a bad first day, folks in those two categories could certainly make the second day considerably worse.

My sources tell me that senior members of Trump's team are now trading tidbits about her background, particularly regarding her time in China. If anything embarrassing were to surface, they don't seem particularly inclined to tamp it down.

Finally, the timing for this spectacle is horrible for Team Red. Republicans are facing increasingly frightening midterm prospects and they need help and the White House already has enough intrigue and speculation involving Susie Wiles future, the alleged exploits of Kimberly Guilfoyle and allegations facing former Kennedy Center leader Rick Grenell.

Well, throw another log onto the fire and grab the Jiffy Pop.

This has the feel of the first Trump term, of Peak Scaramucci, days, of Trump against the world, making rash decisions and navigating the fallout.

After all, Trump often prospers amid the chaos. It's his superpower. The people he hires should be more careful since they surely lack his death-defying capacities.

One longtime and close observer of Trump offers this explanation for Zacharia's appointment: Trump's goal is to 'make the DC establishment howl in hypocritical self-righteous indignation.'

The problem is now this is Trump's DC. It's hard to see the upside.

There is, however, one substantial reason Zacharia might survive: Trump hates being told that someone he likes must go.
news.summary: By any reasonable assessment, President Donald Trump's new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia has gotten off to a rocky start.

news.title: Canada must diversify trade away from the U.S. for security reasons: Freeland
news.text:
OTTAWA — Former deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland says it’s important for national security reasons that Canada do everything it can to diversify trade away from the United States. 

During a discussion at the Council on Foreign Relations in New York on Thursday, Freeland said it’s dangerous to deepen or maintain a close economic relationship with a partner who “openly says they want to take you over.”

U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly mused about turning Canada into the 51st state and, while he ruled out using military force to annex the country in January 2025, has said he would consider using “economic force.”

Even if the U.S. had a president who believed in free trade with Canada, Freeland says being dependent on any one partner is “not a great idea.”

Freeland’s new book, “Unreliable Boyfriend,” was released this week and is part international analysis about the evolving role of the United States and part political memoir.

Its title is a reference to a comment she made on an American talk show in February, when she said the U.S. is “not a very reliable boyfriend right now.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026. 

Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

news.title: CBS News faces $20M defamation lawsuit after misidentifying Maryland teenager in Reflecting Pool report
news.text:
CBS News is facing a defamation lawsuit as a Maryland teenager seeks $20 million in damages, claiming he was falsely identified as a person arrested for vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool’s lining.

The lawsuit, filed on Wednesday in U.S. District Court in the District of Columbia, identified the 15-year-old plaintiff simply as “JV.”

“He was not arrested for vandalizing it. He was not accused by law enforcement of vandalizing it. Yet CBS News broadcast and published a story to a national audience that placed JV’s image alongside the assertion that five people had been arrested for vandalizing and ‘sabotaging’ the Reflecting Pool, thereby falsely portraying JV as one of the perpetrators of a highly publicized federal crime,” the lawsuit stated.

“The accusation was particularly damaging because at all times material to the allegations, the Reflecting Pool renovation and subsequent alleged vandalism of the Reflecting Pool is or has been the subject of intense national attention and political controversy,” the complaint continued. 

“President Donald Trump frequently discusses the Reflecting Pool renovation and publicly condemned those accused of vandalism in extraordinarily harsh terms, stating that they should be ‘prosecuted to the max,’” it added. 

The lawsuit states that CBS “inserted” JV into the controversy and “exposed him to extreme embarrassment, humiliation, and the public condemnation” directed at the actual vandals. 

The lawsuit claims JV’s presence near the Reflecting Pool “was entirely unrelated to the vandalism” and he was simply briefly detained for riding an e-bike in the area.

JV was released without charges and “his detention had nothing whatsoever to do with vandalism or sabotage of the Reflecting Pool.”

“CBS nevertheless used video footage of JV’s detention in its report about the Reflecting Pool vandalism. As CBS anchor Jericka Duncan told viewers that ‘five people have been arrested,’ the video depicted JV in handcuffs,” the lawsuit stated.

“In the version CBS distributed online and through social media, CBS showed JV turning toward the camera with his face fully visible as Duncan made the statement concerning the arrests and then identified one of the alleged perpetrators, David Hearn,” it continued. 

“The visual and verbal presentation published by Defendants unmistakably conveyed the false message that JV was among the persons arrested for vandalizing the Reflecting Pool and further confused JV with Hearn, an adult who was subsequently indicted on a felony charge arising from the vandalism,” the complaint added.

JV’s legal team claimed CBS was aware that the 15-year-old was detained for the e-bike, and not vandalism, because the original video obtained by the network clearly distinguished between the two issues.

“The facts alleged herein demonstrate that CBS either knew its portrayal of JV was false or acted with reckless disregard for whether it was true,” the lawsuit alleged.

“CBS compounded the harm through the manner and breadth of its publication,” it continued. “Although the national television broadcast did not show JV’s face, CBS’s online and social-media version did. It showed his face immediately after depicting his distinctive sweatshirt and while reporting that arrests had been made. JV was readily recognized by friends and acquaintances.”

The lawsuit pointed out that video of the report accumulated at least 1.8 million views on social media alone. JV’s legal team said he has faced “profound” consequences, including embarrassment, humiliation, anxiety, loss of sleep, emotional distress, friends distancing themselves and a continued “fear that CBS’s false accusation will follow him through high school and affect his college admissions, athletic opportunities, employment, and future career.”

The lawsuit noted that CBS issued an on-air correction but said the “belated acknowledgment … cannot undo the publication or erase its consequences.”

CBS News declined comment on pending litigation.

A judge permanently dismissed the Reflecting Pool vandalism case against former Olympian David Hearn, who was accused of damaging the costly $14 million renovation project in June.
news.summary: CBS News faces a $20 million defamation lawsuit after falsely identifying a Maryland teenager as a Reflecting Pool vandal in a national broadcast.

news.title: US senators move to block Saudi nuclear deal
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 16 (IANS) Two Democratic US senators introduced a resolution seeking to block President Donald Trump's civilian nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia, warning that the deal lacks safeguards needed to prevent a nuclear arms race in the Middle East. Senators Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Edward Markey of Massachusetts introduced the joint resolution of disapproval, setting the stage for a Senate vote after November 29, before the proposed agreement takes effect. The move marks a new congressional challenge to the administration's nuclear diplomacy with Riyadh. Under federal law, Congress has a 90-day review period to examine the agreement. Unless Congress adopts a resolution blocking it, the agreement can enter into force after the review period. Merkley, a senior member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said the United States must insist on strong safeguards before transferring civilian nuclear technology to Saudi Arabia. "Giving Saudi Arabia access to US civilian nuclear energy technology without ironclad protections to make sure it doesn’t provide a foundation for a nuclear bomb is unacceptable," Merkley said. "We can’t sleepwalk into a decision this consequential," he said, stressing Congress's responsibility to scrutinise the agreement. Markey went further, warning that the proposed arrangement could destabilise an already volatile region. "The US-Saudi nuclear deal is about megatons, not megawatts," he said. He accused the administration of pursuing an agreement that falls short of established non-proliferation standards, particularly by allowing uranium enrichment without requiring the strongest international inspections. "This deal is the starting gun for a Middle East nuclear arms race. Congress must reject it," Markey said. The senators contend that the agreement fails to meet two safeguards they consider essential. The first is the so-called gold standard for civilian nuclear cooperation, under which a recipient country commits not to enrich uranium or reprocess spent nuclear fuel. Both activities can have legitimate civilian applications but also involve technologies that could contribute to the production of nuclear weapons material. The second is adherence to the International Atomic Energy Agency's Additional Protocol, which provides inspectors with broader access and information to help detect undeclared nuclear activities. According to the senators, the absence of these conditions could create incentives for other regional powers to seek similar concessions. They specifically cited the United Arab Emirates, whose nuclear cooperation agreement with Washington incorporated stronger restrictions on sensitive nuclear activities. The senators warned that offering Saudi Arabia more favourable terms could encourage the UAE to reconsider its existing commitments. They also expressed concern that Iran could resist future restrictions on its nuclear programme if Saudi Arabia were permitted to pursue capabilities denied to Tehran. The proposed resolution would block the US-Saudi agreement if enacted. Its introduction does not, however, suspend the agreement or establish that Congress has rejected it. The initiative follows earlier demands from lawmakers for greater transparency over the proposed agreement, including access to two accompanying side letters that the administration has classified. Civilian nuclear cooperation agreements under Section 123 of the US Atomic Energy Act establish the legal framework for transferring specified nuclear materials, equipment and technology to foreign partners. They are subject to congressional review because of their implications for nuclear non-proliferation and national security.

news.title: Elon Musk’s finger-pointing at Trump backed up by bombshell report
news.text:
Elon Musk's attempt to pin a deadly battlefield decision on President Donald Trump just got backing from an explosive new report.

The directive to throttle Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite service on which Ukrainian troops rely, originated inside the White House, Reuters reported Thursday, citing two U.S. officials and a Western official who had been briefed on the matter.

According to officials, Defense Department leaders were sent a message instructing them to slow the service for Ukraine's military. They did not say who in the White House gave the order or who carried it out.

The report lands a day after Musk publicly laid the blame at the president's feet. Responding on X Wednesday to former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who had pressed him to lift the speed cap, the SpaceX chief insisted his company wasn't calling the shots.

"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk wrote.

The Trump administration pushed back Thursday. Asked about the order, a senior U.S. official told Reuters, "No such request was ever made by the president." The White House didn't answer questions about whether anyone else in the Trump administration was behind it.

A senior Ukrainian official told Reuters that Kyiv spent Tuesday and Wednesday calling senior officials at the White House, State Department and Pentagon looking for an explanation, and was told that the restriction was a White House decision.

The stakes are high. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Piers Morgan Wednesday that people were killed because interceptor drones that depend on Starlink stopped working. Ukrainian officials said the slowdown also hampered strikes on Russian forces and supply lines. A Defense Ministry source told Reuters the receptors are functioning in motion again, but only up to 100 miles per hour.

The clampdown came as Trump has leaned on Kyiv to halt its attacks on Russian oil refineries, which he blames for rising energy prices heading into the midterms. At an October 9 meeting in Miami, Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and envoy Steve Witkoff took a hard line with Ukrainian officials over the strikes, according to a person familiar with the matter.

Musk himself had backed Trump's pressure campaign just days ago, sharing a clip of the president's warning to Zelenskyy on October 10 with the comment, "Zelensky has gone too far."

news.title: Susan Collins' post-heckle debate jab lands on deaf ears: 'Oh, shut up!'
news.text:
An interruption of the final Maine Senate debate between Republican Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson on Wednesday led to a half-testy, half-joking exchange between the two candidates onstage.

The questioning was disrupted when a protester began yelling about data centers, throwing everyone off balance.

"I'm so sorry to interrupt ... I'm terrified," shouted the man, over Collins' attempts to speak. "AI data centers are destroying our climate! They are poisoning our waters!"

As security moved to escort the man out, Collins said, "So, this is obviously one of Troy's supporters."

"Oh shut up," said Jackson, "I don't even know that kid!"

The development of AI data centers has become one of the most hot-button issues in local politics around the country. Many locals, both liberals and conservatives, have fiercely fought their construction, either because they believe it will be a nuisance or a threat to the local environment, or as a proxy for general distrust of the advancement of AI technology. Proponents argue that many of these criticisms are overblown and that data centers bring large amounts of tax revenue to the surrounding area.

President Donald Trump has plowed ahead despite concerns, proclaiming anyone who refuses to let data centers be built are voting for their communities to be poorer.
